name: Mem-α

paper.title: Mem-α: Learning Memory Construction via Reinforcement Learning

construction.unit: core paragraph (≤512 tokens) + semantic fact entries + episodic timestamped event entries
construction.kept_as: written by the agent: facts and events restated from the chunk; core is a running summary
construction.processing: for each incoming chunk the RL-trained agent issues insert / update / delete tool calls on the three stores in one response

organization.structure: three typed stores: core paragraph, semantic list, episodic list
organization.stores: core (always in context), semantic memory, episodic memory
organization.index: BM25 over semantic and episodic entries (embeddings also computed but unused by the default reader)

management.operations: agent chooses insert, update or delete per entry; core can only be rewritten whole; exact duplicate inserts are skipped
management.conflicts: left to the agent, which can edit only entries whose ids it sees (core + 5 newest per list)
management.forgetting: agent-issued delete; core cut at 512 tokens

retrieval.candidates: BM25 separately over semantic and over episodic entries
retrieval.selection: top 20 per store, lowered by 1 until the prompt is under 30K tokens (code)

classify.note: Only the write policy is learned; retrieval is a fixed BM25 top-k and the answer model is frozen.

stages.ingestion: Inputs arrive as a sequence of chunks (dialogues, documents, labelled examples or book passages wrapped as user-assistant turns), processed one at a time.
stages.construction: For each chunk the writer model gets a fixed memorising prompt plus the current core memory and the 5 newest entries of each list, and answers with a batch of insert / update / delete function calls.
stages.organization: Three stores: a core paragraph capped at 512 tokens that is always shown, a semantic list of facts and an episodic list of timestamped events; entries carry short random ids.
stages.update: The agent updates or deletes entries by id and rewrites the core whole; there is no separate consolidation step.
stages.retrieval: At question time BM25 ranks semantic and episodic entries separately against the question and keeps the top 20 of each (fewer if the prompt would exceed 30K tokens).
stages.answer: A frozen Qwen3-32B answers from the core paragraph plus the retrieved entries in a fixed memory prompt.
stages.learning: The writer (Qwen3-4B) is trained with GRPO, without a KL term, on 562 instances of up to 30K tokens; reward = QA accuracy of the final memory + tool-call success + 0.05 × compression + 0.1 × a Qwen3-32B check that each write fits its memory type.

summary: Trains a small model with RL to write a core/semantic/episodic memory through tool calls, rewarding the QA accuracy that a fixed BM25 reader achieves on the final memory; the learned writer generalises from 30K-token training inputs to 400K+.
notes: Venue: arXiv v1 (2025-09-30) is marked 'Preprint'; no venue found in the PDF. Code link from the PDF header ('Source Code') and README: https://github.com/wangyu-ustc/Mem-alpha. headline: Only the memory writer is trained: a 4B model learns by RL which insert / update / delete calls to make; retrieval (BM25) and the answer model (Qwen3-32B) stay fixed.
The reward is the QA accuracy that fixed reader gets from the final memory, plus tool-call success, a compression term and an LLM check that each write fits its store.
While writing, the agent sees only the core paragraph and the 5 newest entries of each list, so it can edit only those.

abstract.text: Mem-α argues that memory agents fail less from missing tools than from not knowing what to store, where, and when to update, and proposes to learn this with reinforcement learning. An agent reads a stream of chunks and writes to a memory made of a core summary, a semantic fact list and an episodic event list through tool calls; after the stream ends, questions are answered from that memory by a fixed retriever and reader, and the accuracy becomes the reward, together with format, compression and content-validity terms. A Qwen3-4B trained this way on a purpose-built dataset beats long-context, BM25 RAG, MemAgent and MEM1 baselines, and although trained on inputs of at most 30K tokens it handles MemoryAgentBench inputs above 400K tokens.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

open_questions: Read budgets differ across methods: RAG-Top2 answers from 2 raw chunks, Long-Context from the last 32K tokens, Mem-α from up to 40 entries plus the core under 30K tokens; the tables cannot separate better writing from a larger reading window.
The paper does not report how many updates and deletes the trained writer issues versus inserts, so how much of the gain is organising versus storing more is open.

discussion.takeaway: Train the memory writer, not the reader: RL on end-task QA accuracy teaches a 4B model to fill a core/semantic/episodic memory well enough to beat long-context and RAG baselines, and the skill carries over to inputs more than 13× longer than any seen in training.

claims.claim: Mem-α beats all baselines on average, in and out of distribution.
claims.evidence: Validation avg 0.642 vs 0.588 (Long-Context) and 0.567 (RAG-Top2); MemoryAgentBench avg 0.592 vs 0.502 and 0.461. Tables 1-2, §4.2

claims.claim: The gain comes from RL, not the memory design.
claims.evidence: Same framework with an untrained Qwen3-4B writer 0.389, with gpt-4.1-mini 0.517, with Mem-α 0.642. Table 3, §4.3

claims.claim: Trained on ≤30K tokens, it generalises to 400K+.
claims.evidence: MemoryAgentBench Multi-Doc inputs reach 474K tokens; Mem-α 0.680 there vs 0.450 RAG-Top2. Table 2, §4.2
γ = 0 drops the validation average to 0.543 (0.445 on MemoryAgentBench). Table 4, Table 9

claims.claim: The compression reward trades memory size for accuracy.
claims.evidence: β 0.2 and 0.4 give 4.7K and 3.6K tokens at 0.525 and 0.509; β 0.05 shrinks BookSum memory from 4.5K to 2.2K at similar accuracy. Table 4, §4.4

claims.claim: Flat single-paragraph memories are not enough.
claims.evidence: MemAgent 0.198 and MEM1 0.071 on MemoryAgentBench. Table 2, §4.2

limits: The memory architecture is simple; richer systems such as MIRIX could help.
Training and evaluation run in simulated settings; real databases and production use raise latency, scalability and safety questions.
Conflict resolution is not trained or evaluated, for lack of realistic benchmarks (§3.4).
Qwen3-8B could not follow the tool format reliably and was dropped (App. C.1).
reading: The 'Mem.' columns count everything stored, not what the reader sees: on MemoryAgentBench Mem-α stores 129K tokens on average, but the reader gets at most core + 20 + 20 entries under 30K tokens (code), while RAG-Top2 reads only 2 raw chunks and Long-Context the last 32K tokens.

Mem-α does not win every set: on MemoryAgentBench it trails Long-Context on NLU (0.710 vs 0.740), Clinic (0.730 vs 0.860) and Banking77 (0.700 vs 0.770) and RAG-Top2 on LME(S*) (0.520 vs 0.581); on validation it trails on HotpotQA, NLU and PubMed.
Table 1 sets are the validation split of the training sources, so they are in-distribution; Table 2 is the out-of-distribution test.
MemAgent answers with its own 14B model, while every other method answers with Qwen3-32B.
When writing, the agent is shown only the 5 newest entries of each list, so updates and deletes can target only recent entries; older contradictions cannot be fixed.
Embeddings (text-embedding-3-small) are computed for every entry but the default reader ranks by BM25 only.
The averages mix different metrics (SubEM, EM, keyword hit, LLM judge), and the LME(S*) judge model is not named.
The paper gives γ = 1 in §4.1 and γ = 0.1 in §4.4; the code and README use 0.1.
